actual_action: States adopted the Montreal Protocol on 16 September 1987, creating binding controls on major ozone-depleting substances with differentiated implementation, reporting and periodic scientific/technical assessment. The agreement entered into force in 1989 and was repeatedly strengthened through later adjustments and amendments as evidence and substitute technologies developed.
later_evidence: The control regime was progressively tightened beyond the original 1987 schedule rather than being treated as a one-time final answer.

A Multilateral Fund was later established to help eligible developing countries meet control obligations through financial and technical assistance, addressing part of the unequal-capacity burden identified during implementation.
The Montreal Protocol achieved universal ratification and the overwhelming majority of controlled ozone-depleting substances have subsequently been phased out.

UNEP/WMO scientific assessment reports that the ozone layer is on a long-term recovery path, with return toward 1980 ozone values projected on different timelines for the global average, Arctic and Antarctic if current policies remain in place.

Later climate science also found major climate co-benefits because many ozone-depleting substances are powerful greenhouse gases; those co-benefits were not necessary to justify the original ozone-protection decision.
outcomes: The staged/reviewable architecture allowed governments to act before every downstream harm was precisely quantified while preserving the ability to strengthen controls as science improved.
Industrial transition occurred rather than the agreement requiring an immediate universal shutdown of all relevant technologies.
Differentiated obligations and later financial/technical assistance reduced, though did not eliminate, fairness concerns for lower-capacity states.
The later recovery evidence is consistent with the original decision being an effective example of international precaution, but that success must remain hidden from first-pass evaluators.
later_reviews_or_findings: This case is retained as a positive environmental control: The Moral Code should be able to support proportionate precautionary regulation when evidence is strong enough to identify a serious plausible harm pathway but exact outcome probabilities remain uncertain.
The case also tests challengeability: policy strength changed as evidence and technology changed rather than the original treaty becoming unquestionable.

Later success should not teach the evaluator a hindsight rule that every environmental restriction is justified; the first-pass case must turn on contemporaneous evidence, severity, reversibility, alternatives and burden distribution.
